claim: Cognitive functions such as working memory (WM) are emergent properties of large-scale network interactions.
source: Cognitive functions such as working memory (WM) are emergent properties of large-scale network interactions.
evidence: This is a general statement about cognitive functions and working memory that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Synchronisation of oscillatory activity might contribute to WM by enabling the coordination of long-range processes.
source: Synchronisation of oscillatory activity might contribute to WM by enabling the coordination of long-range processes.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on existing theoretical frameworks in neuroscience.

claim: Externally induced synchronization improved performance when cognitive demands were high.
source: Externally induced synchronization improved performance when cognitive demands were high.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study showing behavioral improvements during high-demand tasks.

claim: Synchronous tACS during the verbal WM task increased parietal activity, which correlated with behavioral performance.
source: Specifically, synchronous tACS during the verbal WM task increased parietal activity, which correlated with behavioral performance.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data showing increased parietal activity and correlation analyses with behavioral measures.

claim: The relative phase of frontoparietal stimulation influences information flow within the WM network.
source: Furthermore, functional connectivity results indicate that the relative phase of frontoparietal stimulation influences information flow within the WM network.
evidence: This is supported by functional connectivity analyses showing phase-dependent differences in network interactions.

claim: Information exchange within and between networks occurs through the oscillatory synchronization of neuronal activity.
source: A prominent hypothesis is that information exchange within and between networks occurs through the oscillatory synchronization of neuronal activity, such that synchronous neuronal firing binds neurons into ensembles engaged in specific computational functions (Varela et al., 2001; Fries, 2005; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Fries, 2015; Parkin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Rhythmic synchrony increases network efficiency, a process thought to be particularly relevant for demanding cognitive processes such as working memory.
source: Rhythmic synchrony increases network efficiency, a process thought to be particularly relevant for demanding cognitive processes such as working memory (WM) (Fries, 2005; Deco et al., 2011; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Fries, 2015; Constantinidis and Klingberg, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Frontal and parietal brain regions support WM.
source: Frontal and parietal brain regions support WM (Cohen et al., 1997; Prabhakaran et al., 2000; Pessoa et al., 2002; Todd and Marois, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Oscillatory activity in the theta range (4–8 Hz) appears to organize local neuronal ensembles across distant regions during WM processes.
source: Oscillatory activity in the theta range (4–8 Hz) appears to organize local neuronal ensembles across distant regions during WM processes (Buzsáki, 1996; Sarnthein et al., 1998; Rutishauser et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on theta oscillations and working memory.

claim: Theta power increases during complex manipulations of items in WM.
source: Theta power increases during complex manipulations of items in WM (Sauseng et al., 2005), with increasing memory load (Jensen and Tesche, 2002; Payne and Kounios, 2009), and is correlated with WM performance (Jacobs et al., 2006; Fuentemilla et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous empirical studies.

claim: The relative phases of theta oscillations influence encoding and retrieval success.
source: Moreover, the relative phases of these oscillations influence encoding and retrieval success (Rizzuto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Frontoparietal theta synchrony with ~0° phase lag is associated with the maintenance and manipulation of information in WM.
source: For example, frontoparietal theta synchrony with ~0° phase lag is associated with the maintenance and manipulation of information in WM (Sauseng et al., 2005; Polanía et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In- and anti-phase theta frequency (6 Hz) stimulation was applied across two key nodes of the right frontoparietal network: the middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule.
source: In- and anti-phase theta frequency (6 Hz) stimulation was applied across two key nodes of the right frontoparietal network: the middle frontal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Similar tACS stimulation has previously been shown to produce phase-dependent modulations of WM performance.
source: Similar tACS stimulation has previously been shown to produce phase-dependent modulations of WM performance (Polanía et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increasing demand in verbal N-back conditions was associated with stronger activity and effective connectivity within the right hemisphere WM network.
source: The right hemisphere was stimulated because increasing demand in verbal N-back conditions was associated with stronger activity and effective connectivity within the right hemisphere WM network (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Dima et al., 2014), as well as a more pronounced effect of tACS on WM performance (Jaušovec et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: tACS has a more pronounced effect on WM performance in the right hemisphere.
source: The right hemisphere was stimulated because increasing demand in verbal N-back conditions was associated with stronger activity and effective connectivity within the right hemisphere WM network (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Dima et al., 2014), as well as a more pronounced effect of tACS on WM performance (Jaušovec et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Short trains of tACS avoid aftereffects of the stimulation whilst maximizing power to detect changes in the BOLD signal.
source: Our fMRI-tACS experimental design used short trains of tACS that avoid aftereffects of the stimulation (Vossen et al., 2015) whilst maximizing power to detect changes in the blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and describes the methodological rationale.

claim: BOLD provides a measurement of brain activity during tACS without complex artifacts that can severely contaminate traditional EEG and MEG recordings.
source: Functional (f) MRI is well suited to this purpose because BOLD: (1) provides a measurement of brain activity during tACS without complex artifacts that can severely contaminate traditional electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) recordings (Cabral-Calderin et al., 2016; Vosskuhl et al., 2016; Noury et al., 2016);
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on fMRI-tACS methodology.

claim: BOLD is unaffected by the phase of the applied stimulation.
source: and (2) is unaffected by the phase of the applied stimulation.
evidence: This is presented as an established property of BOLD imaging in the context of tACS.

claim: Synchronous (in-phase) stimulation caused an improvement in performance and led to increased frontoparietal activity when cognitive demands were high.
source: We found that synchronous (in-phase) stimulation caused an improvement in performance and led to increased frontoparietal activity when cognitive demands were high.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from both behavioral and fMRI measurements.

claim: External manipulations of large-scale brain synchronization can be used to shape activity and connectivity within brain networks, and those modulations are detectable using fMRI.
source: These results show that external manipulations of large-scale brain synchronization can be used to shape activity and connectivity within brain networks, and those modulations are detectable using fMRI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Underlying cognitive demand has an important influence on the neural effects of tACS.
source: We additionally demonstrate the important influence of underlying cognitive demand on the neural effects of tACS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects across task conditions.

claim: Ten healthy volunteers performed a session of each tACS condition (synchronous, desynchronous and sham) in a pseudo-randomized single-blinded cross-over design.
source: Ten healthy volunteers performed a session of each tACS condition (synchronous, desynchronous and sham) in a pseudo-randomized single-blinded cross-over design.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 1.

claim: There was a significant main effect of task on reaction time in Experiment 1.
source: For RTs, there was a significant main effect of task (F(2,18)=45.47, p<0.001, ηp2=0.84), tACS condition (F(2,18)=8.02, p=0.003, ηp2=0.47) and task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=3.20, p=0.024, ηp2=0.26).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a significant main effect of tACS condition on reaction time in Experiment 1.
source: For RTs, there was a significant main effect of task (F(2,18)=45.47, p<0.001, ηp2=0.84), tACS condition (F(2,18)=8.02, p=0.003, ηp2=0.47) and task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=3.20, p=0.024, ηp2=0.26).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a significant task x tACS condition interaction on reaction time in Experiment 1.
source: For RTs, there was a significant main effect of task (F(2,18)=45.47, p<0.001, ηp2=0.84), tACS condition (F(2,18)=8.02, p=0.003, ηp2=0.47) and task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=3.20, p=0.024, ηp2=0.26).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Synchronous stimulation improved performance on the cognitively demanding 2-back task.
source: Synchronous stimulation improved performance on the cognitively demanding 2-back task. A main effect of tACS condition on RTs was observed (F(2,18)=7.65, p=0.004, ηp2=0.46).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Synchronous tACS resulted in faster responses compared to desynchronous tACS in the 2-back task.
source: This reflected faster responses in the synchronous compared to both the desynchronous (t(9) = −5.72, p<0.001, d = 0.76) and sham conditions (t(9) = −2.43, p=0.038, d = 0.58) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Synchronous tACS resulted in faster responses compared to sham in the 2-back task.
source: This reflected faster responses in the synchronous compared to both the desynchronous (t(9) = −5.72, p<0.001, d = 0.76) and sham conditions (t(9) = −2.43, p=0.038, d = 0.58) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no difference between the RTs in the desynchronous and sham conditions for the 2-back task.
source: In contrast, there was no difference between the RTs in the desynchronous and sham conditions (t(9) = 0.76, p=0.468, d = 0.15).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back condition.
source: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back (F(2,18)=1.11, p=0.351, ηp2=0.11) and CRT (F(2,18)=1.50, p=0.251, ηp2=0.14) conditions, supporting a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and ruling out a simple motor effect.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the CRT condition.
source: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back (F(2,18)=1.11, p=0.351, ηp2=0.11) and CRT (F(2,18)=1.50, p=0.251, ηp2=0.14) conditions, supporting a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and ruling out a simple motor effect.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The absence of tACS effects on less demanding tasks supports a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and rules out a simple motor effect.
source: There was no effect of stimulation on RTs for the less demanding 1-back (F(2,18)=1.11, p=0.351, ηp2=0.11) and CRT (F(2,18)=1.50, p=0.251, ηp2=0.14) conditions, supporting a role for phase synchronization during demanding WM processes and ruling out a simple motor effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: The expected slowing of RTs was observed for 2-back relative to 1-back performance in desynchronous and sham conditions.
source: While the expected slowing of RTs was observed for 2-back relative to 1-back performance in desynchronous and sham conditions (paired t-test between 1-back and 2-back: desynchronous tACS: t(9) = −4.19, p=0.002; sham: t(9) = −3.41, p=0.008), there was no significant difference in performance when the synchronous stimulation was applied (t(9) = −1.88, p=0.093).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was no significant difference in performance between 2-back and 1-back when synchronous stimulation was applied.
source: While the expected slowing of RTs was observed for 2-back relative to 1-back performance in desynchronous and sham conditions (paired t-test between 1-back and 2-back: desynchronous tACS: t(9) = −4.19, p=0.002; sham: t(9) = −3.41, p=0.008), there was no significant difference in performance when the synchronous stimulation was applied (t(9) = −1.88, p=0.093).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Accuracy was unaffected by stimulation in Experiment 1.
source: Accuracy was unaffected by stimulation, as no main effect of tACS condition (F(2,18)=1.01, p=0.383, ηp2=0.10) or task x tACS condition interaction (F(4,36)=0.51, p=0.730, ηp2=0.05) was observed.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a main effect of task condition on accuracy in Experiment 1.
source: As expected, the repeated-measures ANOVA resulted in a main effect of task condition (F(2,18)=15.20, p<0.001, ηp2=0.63), with the 2-back condition showing lower accuracy than the 1-back and CRT conditions (2-back: 83.9% ± 3.7%; 1-back: 95.6% ± 1.5%; CRT: 96.3% ± 0.7%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: The 2-back condition showed lower accuracy than the 1-back and CRT conditions.
source: As expected, the repeated-measures ANOVA resulted in a main effect of task condition (F(2,18)=15.20, p<0.001, ηp2=0.63), with the 2-back condition showing lower accuracy than the 1-back and CRT conditions (2-back: 83.9% ± 3.7%; 1-back: 95.6% ± 1.5%; CRT: 96.3% ± 0.7%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Twenty-four participants underwent a session of simultaneous tACS-fMRI in Experiment 2.
source: Twenty-four participants underwent a session of simultaneous tACS-fMRI (Figure 2A) in which they performed separate runs of blocked 2-back and CRT tasks, for both the synchronous (0° relative phase) and desynchronous (180° relative phase) tACS conditions (N = 21 for 2-back task and N = 20 for CRT task, see Materials and methods for exclusion criteria).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 2.

claim: TACS stimulation did not significantly impact behavior across stimulation conditions in Experiment 2.
source: TACS stimulation did not significantly impact behavior across stimulation conditions, consistent with its use as a physiological probe (Driver et al., 2009; Fedorenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and citations to similar methodological approaches.

claim: There was no significant main effect of tACS condition on RTs or accuracy in Experiment 2.
source: There was no significant main effect of tACS condition on RTs or accuracy, or interaction between task (2-back and CRT) and tACS condition (all F values < 1, all p values > 0.4).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a main effect of task on RTs in Experiment 2.
source: As expected, there was a main effect of task on RTs (F(1,18)=73.16, p<0.001, ηp2=0.80) and accuracy (F(1,18)=81.68, p<0.001, ηp2=0.82), driven by slower responses (2-back: 0.66 ± 0.24 s; CRT: 0.44 ± 0.1 s) and reduced accuracy (2-back: 80.2% ± 1.7%; CRT: 97.1% ± 0.8%) in the 2-back than in the CRT task conditions, attributable to the expected differences in task difficulty.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: There was a main effect of task on accuracy in Experiment 2.
source: As expected, there was a main effect of task on RTs (F(1,18)=73.16, p<0.001, ηp2=0.80) and accuracy (F(1,18)=81.68, p<0.001, ηp2=0.82), driven by slower responses (2-back: 0.66 ± 0.24 s; CRT: 0.44 ± 0.1 s) and reduced accuracy (2-back: 80.2% ± 1.7%; CRT: 97.1% ± 0.8%) in the 2-back than in the CRT task conditions, attributable to the expected differences in task difficulty.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: 2-back performance was associated with increased BOLD signal in visual cortex, caudate, thalamus, cerebellum, lateral premotor cortex, dorsal cingulate and medial premotor cortex, dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, frontal poles and medial and lateral posterior parietal cortex.
source: 2-back performance was associated with increased BOLD signal in visual cortex, caudate, thalamus, cerebellum, lateral premotor cortex, dorsal cingulate and medial premotor cortex, dorsolateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, frontal poles and medial and lateral posterior parietal cortex (Figure 3A, left).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CRT performance was associated with increased activity within bilateral sensory motor regions, as well as in the supplementary motor area, visual cortex, thalamus and the putamen.
source: CRT performance was associated with increased activity within bilateral sensory motor regions, as well as in the supplementary motor area, visual cortex, thalamus and the putamen (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The activity in the frontoparietal networks was higher for the 2-back than for the CRT task.
source: As expected, the activity in the frontoparietal networks was higher for the 2-back than for the CRT task.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Deactivation of the default mode network (DMN) regions was observed for both the CRT and 2-back tasks compared to rest.
source: Deactivation of the default mode network (DMN) regions was observed for both the CRT and 2-back tasks compared to rest, with extensive deactivation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and frontal orbital cortex seen during 2-back performance (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Task-related BOLD responses were increased in the IPL and MFG regions for the synchronous tACS condition selectively during performance of the 2-back task.
source: Task-related BOLD responses were increased in the IPL and MFG regions for the synchronous tACS condition (tACS 0° > tACS OFF) selectively during performance of the 2-back task (Figure 3B), but not during the desynchronous tACS condition (tACS 180° > tACS OFF).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A negative correlation was observed between participants' mean BOLD signal in the IPL-electrode region and their mean RTs during synchronous tACS.
source: A negative correlation was observed between participants' mean BOLD signal in the IPL-electrode region and their mean RTs during synchronous tACS (r(21)= −0.39, p=0.039, one-tailed), indicating that across participants increased brain activity related to reduced RTs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fMRI and behavioral data and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No correlation was observed between BOLD signal in the MFG-electrode region and RTs during synchronous tACS.
source: No correlation was observed for the MFG-electrode region (r(21)= −0.29, p=0.103, one-tailed).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fMRI and behavioral data.

claim: During performance of the CRT task, the BOLD response was increased only for the synchronous tACS condition and exclusively in the MFG-electrode region.
source: During performance of the CRT task, the BOLD response was increased only for the synchronous tACS condition (tACS 0° > tACS OFF) and exclusively in the MFG-electrode region (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No correlation was observed between the increased BOLD response in the MFG and RTs during synchronous tACS in the CRT task.
source: No correlation was observed between the increased BOLD response in the MFG and RTs during synchronous tACS.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fMRI and behavioral data.

claim: There was no difference in BOLD signal in the return electrode region (T8) in any of the tACS or task conditions.
source: Furthermore, to test whether the measured effects of tACS on brain activity could be explained by a simple direct effect of the electric current on the BOLD signal, we investigated activity in the brain region corresponding to the return electrode (electrode at T8, over the right middle temporal gyrus, Figure 1A). There was no difference in BOLD signal for this region in any of the tACS or task conditions.
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: During fixation periods with tACS stimulation, neither the synchronous nor the desynchronous tACS conditions elicited differences in BOLD signal compared to baseline.
source: Similarly, during fixation periods with tACS stimulation, neither the synchronous nor the desynchronous tACS conditions elicited differences in BOLD signal compared to baseline (fixation periods without stimulation), for either the 2-back or the CRT tasks.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Synchronous tACS applied during performance of the 2-back task increased neural activity in the right frontoparietal network.
source: Synchronous tACS applied during performance of the 2-back task had a widespread effect on regions normally activated by task performance (tACS 0° > tACS OFF). Neural activity increased in the right frontoparietal network, with peaks of increased BOLD activity seen in the right lateral prefrontal cortex, middle frontal gyrus and bilaterally in the posterior parietal cortices
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis.

claim: Synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased BOLD activity bilaterally in the thalamus, basal ganglia, occipital cortex and inferior temporal gyrus.
source: Additionally, BOLD activity increases were seen bilaterally in the thalamus, basal ganglia, occipital cortex and inferior temporal gyrus (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Desynchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased deactivation in parts of the default mode network.
source: A distinct pattern was observed for the desynchronous tACS condition. Increased deactivation (tACS 180° < tACS OFF) was observed in parts of the default mode network (DMN), namely the posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, ventromedial PFC, left orbitofrontal cortex and left parahippocampal gyrus (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Direct contrast of synchronous and desynchronous stimulation revealed differences in the left hemisphere inferior parietal lobule (IPL), superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC).
source: We directly contrasted synchronous and desynchronous stimulation using the contrast (tACS 0° > tACS OFF) > (tACS 180° > tACS OFF). This revealed differences induced by the two tACS phase conditions in the left hemisphere inferior parietal lobule (IPL), superior frontal gyrus (SFG) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), Figure 4C, explained by increased deactivation for the desynchronous compared to the synchronous tACS condition (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The less demanding CRT task resulted in similar increases in BOLD activity in the occipital cortex for both synchronous and desynchronous tACS.
source: The less demanding CRT task resulted in similar increases in BOLD activity in the occipital cortex for both synchronous and desynchronous tACS.
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis.

claim: Desynchronous tACS during the CRT task increased BOLD signal in the supplementary motor cortex.
source: Additionally, increased BOLD signal was observed for the supplementary motor cortex during the desynchronous tACS condition and right frontal orbital/insular cortex for the synchronous condition (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1, tables supplement 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Synchronous tACS during the CRT task increased BOLD signal in the right frontal orbital/insular cortex.
source: Additionally, increased BOLD signal was observed for the supplementary motor cortex during the desynchronous tACS condition and right frontal orbital/insular cortex for the synchronous condition (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 1, tables supplement 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No differences in the contrasts for synchronous vs desynchronous stimulation were observed for the CRT task.
source: No differences in the contrasts for synchronous vs desynchronous stimulation were observed for the CRT task.
evidence: This is supported by whole-brain fMRI data analysis.

claim: Externally inducing synchronization or desynchronization of the right frontoparietal network modulates activity across large-scale networks in a cognitive state dependent manner.
source: These results show that externally inducing synchronization or desynchronization of the right frontoparietal network modulates activity across large-scale networks in a cognitive state dependent manner, such that phase dependent effects were observed clearly for the 2-back task, when cognitive demands were high.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of fMRI results across different task conditions.

claim: During fixation periods with simultaneous tACS stimulation, no increases in the BOLD signal compared to baseline were observed.
source: This was further confirmed during fixation periods with simultaneous tACS stimulation. For this condition, we observed no increases in the BOLD signal compared to baseline (fixation periods without tACS).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Increased deactivation was observed during fixation with tACS in a number of brain regions, but there were no phase dependent differences during the CRT or 2-back runs.
source: Increased deactivation was observed in a number of brain regions, but there were no phase dependent differences during the CRT or 2-back runs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased FC between the right IPL and posterior parts of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).
source: Synchronous tACS during the 2-back task increased FC between the right IPL and posterior parts of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 6) compared to the FC observed during task performance in the absence of stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 5.

claim: No modulation of FC was observed for the MFG-electrode seed during synchronous tACS in the 2-back task.
source: In contrast, no modulation of FC was observed for the MFG-electrode seed.
evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Desynchronous tACS produced increases in FC in occipito/temporal regions in a similar pattern for both MFG- and IPL-electrode seeds.
source: Desynchronous tACS produced increases in FC in occipito/temporal regions in a similar pattern for both MFG- and IPL-electrode seeds (Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1, table supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data and shown in Figure 5.

claim: There was no correlation between FC in the 2-back task and RTs.
source: There was no correlation between FC in the 2-back task and RTs.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of functional connectivity and behavioral data.

claim: The tACS phase dependent modulation of FC observed for the 2-back task was absent for the CRT task.
source: The tACS phase dependent modulation of FC observed for the 2-back task was absent for the CRT task, where no modulations of FC were observed.
evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Functional connectivity using the return electrode region as seed did not show any modulations in FC in either the 2-back or CRT tasks.
source: As a control, we also investigated functional connectivity using the return electrode region as seed, which did not show any modulations in FC in either the 2-back or CRT tasks.
evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: No modulation of FC was observed during fixation periods using any of the seed regions for any tACS or task conditions.
source: Furthermore, no modulation of FC was observed during fixation periods using any of the seed regions for any tACS or task conditions.
evidence: This is supported by PPI analysis of fMRI data.

claim: There was very low movement in the fMRI sample.
source: Overall, there was very low movement in our sample (mean framewise displacement (FD) for 2-back = 0.044 ± 0.013, n = 21, and CRT = 0.040 ± 0.011, n = 20)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of motion parameters from fMRI data.

claim: There was no difference in framewise displacement between periods with and without stimulation or for different tACS phase conditions for any of the tasks.
source: and there was no difference in FD between periods with and without stimulation or for different tACS phase conditions for any of the tasks (Repeated measures ANOVA for CRT and 2-back with factors stimulation (ON, OFF) and tACS phase (0°, 180°); all F values < 2, all p values > 0.2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of motion parameters.

claim: Heart rate was not different between periods with and without stimulation or between different tACS phase conditions.
source: Similarly, heart rate (available for a subset of participants; N = 6) was not different between periods with and without stimulation or between different tACS phase conditions (Repeated measures ANOVA for CRT and 2-back with factors stimulation (ON, OFF) and tACS phase (0°, 180°); all F values < 2, all p values > 0.4).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of physiological monitoring data.

claim: Participants were unaware whether or not they were receiving stimulation and could not distinguish between the type of stimulation.
source: In addition, analysis of post-experiment questionnaires showed that participants were unaware whether or not they were receiving stimulation and could not distinguish between the type of stimulation (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: External manipulations of oscillatory synchrony across a right-sided frontoparietal network impact neural activity and modify behavior.
source: Our results demonstrate that external manipulations of oscillatory synchrony across a right-sided frontoparietal network impact neural activity and modify behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The effects of tACS depend on the relative phase of the external oscillators and also the underlying cognitive state at the time tACS is applied.
source: The effects depend on the relative phase of the external oscillators and also the underlying cognitive state at the time tACS is applied.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing differential effects across phase and task conditions.

claim: Imposing theta frequency synchronously across the inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus improves verbal WM performance and increases frontal and parietal brain activity.
source: In particular, we showed that imposing theta frequency synchronously across the inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus improves verbal WM performance and increases frontal and parietal brain activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the behavioral and fMRI results.

claim: The functional connectivity of the inferior parietal lobe was modulated by tACS in a phase dependent manner.
source: The functional connectivity of the inferior parietal lobe was also modulated by tACS in a phase dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claim: Frontal interactions increased with synchronous theta stimulation whereas posterior interactions increased with desynchronous stimulation.
source: Frontal interactions increased with synchronous theta stimulation whereas posterior interactions increased with desynchronous stimulation, suggesting that information flow through brain regions involved in WM can be differentially affected by varying the phase of external stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claim: Information flow through brain regions involved in WM can be differentially affected by varying the phase of external stimulation.
source: Frontal interactions increased with synchronous theta stimulation whereas posterior interactions increased with desynchronous stimulation, suggesting that information flow through brain regions involved in WM can be differentially affected by varying the phase of external stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claim: tACS interacts with ongoing oscillations and the resultant neural modulations spread along brain networks.
source: It has been proposed that tACS interacts with ongoing oscillations and the resultant neural modulations spread along brain networks (Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010; Ali et al., 2013), with entrainment being more effective when the induced frequency matches the endogenous rhythm (Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010; Reato et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and modeling work.

claim: Entrainment by tACS is more effective when the induced frequency matches the endogenous rhythm.
source: It has been proposed that tACS interacts with ongoing oscillations and the resultant neural modulations spread along brain networks (Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010; Ali et al., 2013), with entrainment being more effective when the induced frequency matches the endogenous rhythm (Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010; Reato et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: tACS stimulation is highly dependent on the underlying network dynamics.
source: This leads to the prediction that stimulation is highly dependent on the underlying network dynamics (Alagapan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and represents a theoretical prediction.

claim: The imaging results for the 2-back and CRT tasks strongly support the notion that the physiological effect of external oscillatory manipulations are highly dependent on the underlying cognitive state.
source: Our imaging results for the 2-back and CRT tasks strongly support these notions and show how the physiological effect of external oscillatory manipulations are highly dependent on the underlying cognitive state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential effects observed across task conditions.

claim: Compared to the CRT, the 2-back task is more demanding and engages the frontoparietal network more heavily.
source: Compared to the CRT, the 2-back task is more demanding and engages the frontoparietal network more heavily, which is observed both in terms of increased BOLD activity and theta power (Payne and Kounios, 2009; Heinzel et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by the current study's data and citations to previous research.

claim: The behavioral findings strongly suggest a causal link between theta phase coupling in the frontoparietal network and cognition.
source: Our behavioral findings strongly suggest a causal link between theta phase coupling in the frontoparietal network and cognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral results showing phase-dependent effects on performance.

claim: The cognitive enhancement produced by synchronous tACS is dependent on the demands of the cognitive task.
source: We replicate the observation that synchronous tACS applied across the frontoparietal networks improves WM performance (Polanía et al., 2012), and extend these results by showing that this cognitive enhancement is dependent on the demands of the cognitive task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of behavioral results across different task difficulty levels.

claim: The observation that tACS had no effect on less demanding 1-back or CRT tasks suggests that the behavioral effects of entraining oscillations interacts with the extent that a network is already engaged by a cognitive task.
source: Our observations that tACS had no effect on less demanding 1-back or CRT tasks suggests that the behavioral effects of entraining oscillations interacts with the extent that a network is already engaged by a cognitive task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: Synchronous tACS produced sufficient improvement in response times to make 2-back performance similar to the 1-back condition.
source: Remarkably, synchronous tACS produced sufficient improvement in response times to make 2-back performance similar to the 1-back condition, which is typically associated with much faster responses.
evidence: This is supported by the behavioral data showing no significant difference between 2-back and 1-back RTs during synchronous stimulation.

claim: Increased rhythmic synchrony across a network is thought to improve information processing by increasing network efficiency.
source: Increased rhythmic synchrony across a network is thought to improve information processing by increasing network efficiency, an effect particularly important during demanding cognitive processing (Fries, 2005, 2009; Deco et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Theta synchrony between frontal and parietal brain regions increases during complex manipulations of items held in WM.
source: For example, theta synchrony between frontal and parietal brain regions increases during complex manipulations of items held in WM (Sauseng et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The neuroimaging results show the neural correlates of the effect of network efficiency on working memory.
source: Importantly, our neuroimaging results show the neural correlates of this effect on network efficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fMRI results showing increased activity and connectivity.

claim: The inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus play a key role in WM function.
source: Entraining synchronous activity across the right frontoparietal network was associated with increased activity within the inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus, regions known to play a key role in WM function.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Activation in the inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus increases with WM demands.
source: Activation in these regions increases with WM demands and its damage leads to impairments of WM (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2004; Berryhill and Olson, 2008; Fedorenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Damage to the inferior parietal lobe and middle frontal gyrus leads to impairments of WM.
source: Activation in these regions increases with WM demands and its damage leads to impairments of WM (Curtis and D'Esposito, 2004; Berryhill and Olson, 2008; Fedorenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The correlation between increased activity within the right inferior parietal lobe and faster responses supports a link between neural activity and the behavioral effects of tACS.
source: In keeping with these findings, we show that increased activity within the right inferior parietal lobe correlated with faster responses during the 2-back, supporting a link between neural activity and the behavioral effects of tACS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: The right inferior parietal lobe plays a critical role during WM maintenance.
source: This is in agreement with the critical role of this region during WM maintenance (Constantinidis and Steinmetz, 1996; Pessoa et al., 2002), and the observations that disrupting its activity through transcranial magnetic stimulation affects performance in both spatial and verbal WM tasks (Kessels et al., 2000; Mottaghy et al., 2003; Postle et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Disrupting the activity of the right inferior parietal lobe through transcranial magnetic stimulation affects performance in both spatial and verbal WM tasks.
source: This is in agreement with the critical role of this region during WM maintenance (Constantinidis and Steinmetz, 1996; Pessoa et al., 2002), and the observations that disrupting its activity through transcranial magnetic stimulation affects performance in both spatial and verbal WM tasks (Kessels et al., 2000; Mottaghy et al., 2003; Postle et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During maintenance of items in WM the parietal cortex is positively associated with trial-by-trial performance and inter-individual differences in WM capacity.
source: Furthermore, during maintenance of items in WM the parietal cortex is positively associated with trial-by-trial performance and inter-individual differences in WM capacity (Todd and Marois, 2004; Xu and Chun, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Parietal and frontal cortices have different contributions to phonological storage and executive control in verbal WM.
source: The fact that a relationship with response times was observed for the parietal but not the frontal region might be explained by the different roles attributed to parietal and frontal cortices in verbal WM. Evidence suggests that these regions have different contributions to phonological storage and executive control (Paulesu et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research and is used to explain the current findings.

claim: The results are congruent with findings showing correlations between BOLD activity or connectivity density and response times in similar verbal WM tasks.
source: Moreover, our results are congruent with findings from other studies showing correlations between BOLD activity or connectivity density and response times in similar verbal WM tasks (Honey et al., 2000; Tomasi et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: By increasing neural activity in the parietal region, tACS might have interacted with the physiological mechanisms associated with response production.
source: Thus, by increasing neural activity in the parietal region, tACS might have interacted with the physiological mechanisms associated with response production.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The changes in BOLD observed were not constrained to regions close to the stimulation sites but showed a more general effect across salience, visuospatial and basal ganglia networks.
source: Importantly, the changes in BOLD we observed were not constrained to regions close to the stimulation sites. Rather a more general effect across salience, visuospatial and basal ganglia networks was seen, which are all regions involved in WM performance (Pessoa et al., 2002; Owen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the whole-brain fMRI analysis and citations to previous research on WM networks.

claim: The stimulant drug methylphenidate has been shown to enhance WM performance and increase parietal activity in a similar verbal N-back task.
source: Interestingly, the stimulant drug methylphenidate has been shown to enhance WM performance and increase parietal activity in a similar verbal N-back task (Tomasi et al., 2011), suggesting that cognitive enhancement produced pharmacologically or electrically may converge on similar neural mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cognitive enhancement produced pharmacologically or electrically may converge on similar neural mechanisms.
source: Interestingly, the stimulant drug methylphenidate has been shown to enhance WM performance and increase parietal activity in a similar verbal N-back task (Tomasi et al., 2011), suggesting that cognitive enhancement produced pharmacologically or electrically may converge on similar neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from comparing the current results with previous pharmacological studies.

claim: The effects of tACS on functional connectivity may inform the mechanisms by which oscillations modulate long-range connectivity.
source: As the maintenance of information in WM relies on the coordination of distant brain regions, the effects of tACS on functional connectivity may inform the mechanisms by which oscillations modulate long-range connectivity.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential implications of the functional connectivity findings.

claim: Increased frontoparietal functional connectivity has previously been observed during WM processing.
source: Increased frontoparietal functional connectivity has previously been observed during WM processing (Fell and Axmacher, 2011), is associated with higher accuracy and faster RTs (Prado et al., 2011), and is linked to increased theta synchrony (Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased frontoparietal functional connectivity is associated with higher accuracy and faster RTs.
source: Increased frontoparietal functional connectivity has previously been observed during WM processing (Fell and Axmacher, 2011), is associated with higher accuracy and faster RTs (Prado et al., 2011), and is linked to increased theta synchrony (Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increased frontoparietal functional connectivity is linked to increased theta synchrony.
source: Increased frontoparietal functional connectivity has previously been observed during WM processing (Fell and Axmacher, 2011), is associated with higher accuracy and faster RTs (Prado et al., 2011), and is linked to increased theta synchrony (Liebe et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Externally induced theta synchrony can increase frontoparietal interactions between the parietal cortex and DLPFC that are important for WM processing.
source: Our results extend these findings by showing how externally induced theta synchrony can increase frontoparietal interactions between the parietal cortex and DLPFC that are important for WM processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claim: Functional connectivity between the frontal region and other brain regions may have been operating at peak levels in the task periods without stimulation and could not be further modulated by tACS.
source: One possible explanation for this finding is that functional connectivity between the frontal and other brain regions was already operating at peak levels in the task periods without stimulation and could not be further modulated by tACS.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the asymmetric connectivity findings.

claim: Distinct frequency channels may be responsible for carrying feedforward and feedback signalling.
source: A more intriguing possibility is that distinct frequency channels are responsible for carrying feedforward and feedback signalling.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain the findings.

claim: In the visual cortex, feedforward influences are carried by theta and gamma band synchronization, while feedback influences by beta band synchronization.
source: Such a distinction has been observed in the visual cortex, where feedforward influences are carried by theta and gamma band synchronization, while feedback influences by beta band synchronization (Bastos et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: tACS applied at the theta frequency might differentially enhance feedforward connectivity across the synchronized fronto-parietal network.
source: In this framework, it is possible that tACS applied at the theta frequency would differentially enhance feedforward connectivity across the synchronized fronto-parietal network.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the framework of frequency-specific directional communication.

claim: Desynchronous tACS was associated with increased connectivity to occipital regions, which could suggest an increase in information exchange between higher- and low-level areas.
source: While synchronous stimulation resulted in increased functional connectivity between parietal and frontal areas, desynchronous tACS was associated with increased connectivity to occipital regions, which could suggest an increase in information exchange between higher- and low-level areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional connectivity results.

claim: Altering phase synchrony might control long-range network interactions and shape information flow.
source: The shift in parietal functional connectivity between frontal and posterior regions shows how altering phase synchrony might control long-range network interactions and so shape information flow.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claim: High WM demands are normally associated with high levels of frontoparietal connectivity, and this can be enhanced by synchronous tACS applied across the network.
source: One interpretation of our findings is that high WM demands are normally associated with high levels of frontoparietal connectivity, and this can be enhanced by synchronous tACS applied across the network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Disrupting interactions across the network through desynchronous tACS increases parietal connections to the occipital lobe, perhaps as a result of the restoration of a 'default' pattern of functional connectivity.
source: Disrupting interactions across the network through desynchronous tACS increases parietal connections to the occipital lobe, perhaps as a result of the restoration of a 'default' pattern of functional connectivity normally observed in the absence of high levels of top-down cognitive control.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional connectivity results.

claim: Phase relations among neuronal groups could contribute to selective routing of information and shape effective connectivity.
source: This idea is supported by the notion that phase relations among neuronal groups could contribute to selective routing of information and shape effective connectivity, an argument supported by computational models (Akam and Kullmann, 2014) and empirical evidence (Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Helfrich et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous computational and empirical research.

claim: Altered phase relations between brain regions precede changes in neural activity.
source: Intracortical recordings show that altered phase relations between brain regions precede changes in neural activity, providing evidence that the influence of synchronizing activity across neuronal groups can be phase dependent (Womelsdorf et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In- and out-of-phase tACS applied in the gamma band modulates inter-hemispheric connectivity and shapes visual perception.
source: Converging evidence that this can be externally modulated is provided by the observation that in- and out-of-phase tACS applied in the gamma band modulates inter-hemispheric connectivity and shapes visual perception (Helfrich et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There is unbalanced electric field distribution between the tACS conditions due to using a common return electrode.
source: First, there is unbalanced electric field distribution between the tACS conditions (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is a consequence of using a common return electrode.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological limitation and is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When current was applied synchronously to the frontal and parietal electrodes the temporal return electrode received the sum of the applied currents to each electrode.
source: Thus, when current was applied synchronously to the frontal and parietal electrodes the temporal return electrode received the sum of the applied currents to each electrode, while in the desynchronous condition the current in the return electrode is cancelled by the opposing phases of the frontal and parietal electrodes.
evidence: This is a description of the electrical properties of the stimulation montage.

claim: The results could not have been predicted by a current density model despite different current distributions between synchronous and desynchronous tACS.
source: Nevertheless, although synchronous and desynchronous tACS resulted in different current distributions in the brain, our results could not have been predicted by a current density model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the modeling results with the empirical findings.

claim: Modulations of brain activity and connectivity were predominantly restricted to areas involved in task performance.
source: Modulations of brain activity and connectivity were predominantly restricted to areas involved in task performance and no effects were observed in the cortical area underneath the temporal return electrode.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI analysis results.

claim: No effects were observed in the cortical area underneath the temporal return electrode.
source: Modulations of brain activity and connectivity were predominantly restricted to areas involved in task performance and no effects were observed in the cortical area underneath the temporal return electrode.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI analysis results.

claim: The results demonstrate that the effects of brain stimulation cannot be determined without taking into account the underlying brain dynamics.
source: These results further demonstrate that the effects of brain stimulation cannot be determined without taking into account the underlying brain dynamics (Reato et al., 2013) and provide additional support for the critical neural state-dependency of tACS (Feurra et al., 2013; Ruhnau et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The area of stimulation was relatively large and potentially affected subregions with complex functional architecture and diverse effects on WM processing.
source: Second, the area of stimulation was relatively large and potentially affected subregions with complex functional architecture and diverse effects on WM processing.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological limitation.

claim: The optimal frequency and phase of tACS is likely to suffer from inter-individual variability.
source: Third, the optimal frequency and phase is likely to suffer from inter-individual variability.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation based on general knowledge about individual differences.

claim: Other combinations of tACS parameters (frequency, phase, intensity, etc.) will likely produce greater effects on cognition.
source: However, the parameter space of possible stimulation regimes is very large and it is likely that other combinations of tACS parameters (that is, frequency, phase, intensity, etc.) will produce greater effects on cognition.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future possibilities.

claim: Machine-learning techniques combined with real-time imaging could help select the ideal combination of parameters to induce the desired modulation of brain activity/connectivity in a subject-specific manner.
source: The key to unlocking the potential of this technique for clinical use will be to understand the neural mechanisms governing the cognitive effects of the stimulation. Machine-learning techniques combined with real-time imaging could help select the ideal combination of parameters to induce the desired modulation of brain activity/connectivity in a subject-specific manner (Lorenz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future methodological approaches, supported by a citation.

claim: The fMRI approach benefited from good spatial resolution in the absence of complex electrical artifacts.
source: Finally, while our fMRI approach benefited from good spatial resolution in the absence of complex electrical artifacts, we are not able to specify which brain frequencies were modulated by our intervention, as the correspondence between brain oscillations and BOLD signal is not fully understood (Scheeringa et al., 2011) and tACS might induce cross-frequency coupling (Reato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the methodological approach.

claim: The study is not able to specify which brain frequencies were modulated by the tACS intervention.
source: Finally, while our fMRI approach benefited from good spatial resolution in the absence of complex electrical artifacts, we are not able to specify which brain frequencies were modulated by our intervention, as the correspondence between brain oscillations and BOLD signal is not fully understood (Scheeringa et al., 2011) and tACS might induce cross-frequency coupling (Reato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study, supported by citations.

claim: The correspondence between brain oscillations and BOLD signal is not fully understood.
source: Finally, while our fMRI approach benefited from good spatial resolution in the absence of complex electrical artifacts, we are not able to specify which brain frequencies were modulated by our intervention, as the correspondence between brain oscillations and BOLD signal is not fully understood (Scheeringa et al., 2011) and tACS might induce cross-frequency coupling (Reato et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: tACS might induce cross-frequency coupling.
source: Finally, while our fMRI approach benefited from good spatial resolution in the absence of complex electrical artifacts, we are not able to specify which brain frequencies were modulated by our intervention, as the correspondence between brain oscillations and BOLD signal is not fully understood (Scheeringa et al., 2011) and tACS might induce cross-frequency coupling (Reato et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Other forms of non-invasive transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), particularly transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) modulate WM performance.
source: Other studies have shown that additional forms of non-invasive transcranial electrical stimulation (tES), particularly transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) modulate WM performance.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from previous research.

claim: The majority of tDCS studies on WM targeted the DLPFC.
source: The majority of these studies targeted the DLPFC and recent meta-analyses have indicated small but significant effects of tDCS on WM (Brunoni and Vanderhasselt, 2014; Hill et al., 2016; Mancuso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analyses.

claim: Recent meta-analyses have indicated small but significant effects of tDCS on WM.
source: The majority of these studies targeted the DLPFC and recent meta-analyses have indicated small but significant effects of tDCS on WM (Brunoni and Vanderhasselt, 2014; Hill et al., 2016; Mancuso et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analyses.

claim: tES is capable of modulating the neural processes associated with WM.
source: Broadly, these findings and ours show that tES is capable of modulating the neural processes associated with WM.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the current study and previous research.

claim: Anodal tDCS applied to the DLPFC increased oscillatory brain activity in alpha and theta frequency bands in occipito-parietal regions during a verbal WM task.
source: Although tDCS uses direct instead of an oscillatory current to modulate cortical excitability, anodal tDCS applied to the DLPFC increased oscillatory brain activity in alpha and theta frequency bands in occipito-parietal regions during a verbal WM task (Zaehle et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Local changes in neuronal excitability induced by tDCS produced interactive effects that resulted in the modulation of oscillatory activity in distant cortical regions.
source: This indicates that the local changes in neuronal excitability induced by tDCS produced interactive effects that resulted in the modulation of oscillatory activity in distant cortical regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research.

claim: Different tES modalities impact brain excitability to different degrees.
source: Although this shows that tDCS interacts with the neural mechanisms associated with WM, future studies should carefully consider the biological processes they aim to target, as different tES modalities impact brain excitability to different degrees (Inukai et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: WM performance is very sensitive to the external stimulation parameters.
source: Furthermore, a recent study elegantly demonstrated that WM performance is very sensitive to the external stimulation parameters (Alekseichuk et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The findings indicate a direct link between behavioral performance in a demanding working-memory task and large-scale brain synchronization across a right frontoparietal network activated by the task.
source: Overall, our findings indicate a direct link between behavioral performance in a demanding working-memory task and large-scale brain synchronization across a right frontoparietal network activated by the task.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental results.

claim: Manipulations of tACS phase modulate the underlying brain activity.
source: We showed how manipulations of tACS phase modulate the underlying brain activity and that tACS can influence long-range connectivity in a phase- and brain state- dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the fMRI results.

claim: tACS can influence long-range connectivity in a phase- and brain state- dependent manner.
source: We showed how manipulations of tACS phase modulate the underlying brain activity and that tACS can influence long-range connectivity in a phase- and brain state- dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the functional connectivity results.

claim: The work shows the potential of performing simultaneous tACS-fMRI to understand the neural mechanisms underlying externally induced oscillatory synchronization.
source: More generally, our work shows the potential of performing simultaneous tACS-fMRI to understand the neural mechanisms underlying externally induced oscillatory synchronization.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.
